ev.text: Идеальным примером, где место ударения зависит от фонетического фактора, является коми-язьвинский диалект. В неодносложных словах этого диалекта ударение не падает на гласные исконно верхнего подъема 1-го слога (i < *i, u < *u, ө < *i̮) — в этом случае акцент находится на каком-нибудь гласном непервого слога. Если же в первом слоге стоят гласные исконно среднего или нижнего подъема (e, o, ȯ, a, u < *o̭, ɯ < *ȯ̭), то ударение падает на них. Таким образом ударение падает на более звучные гласные, т. е. место ударения в слове зависит от качества (сонорности) гласных, наличествующих в этом слове. Мы такое ударение называем качественно-вокальным, например: mu 'земля', muśa·ń 'от земли'; va 'вода…

3990.dq: В неодносложных словах этого диалекта ударение не падает на гласные исконно верхнего подъема 1-го слога ... Таким образом ударение падает на более звучные гласные, т. е. место ударения в слове зависит от качества (сонорности) гласных, наличествующих в этом слове. (p. 250; the article's subject is 'лексическое ударение', and the examples are inflected word forms: mu ~ muśa·ń, va ~ va·śań, muni·s)
3990.heavy: Heavy = 'гласные исконно среднего или нижнего подъема' (e, o, ȯ, a, u < *o̭, ɯ < *ȯ̭; p. 252 adds i < *ḙ), i.e. the 'более звучные' (more sonorous) vowels; light = 'гласные исконно верхнего подъема' (i < *i, u < *u, ө < *i̮), the 'слабосонорные' vowels, with ө behaving as high although phonetically mid today. Weight is vowel height/sonority as fixed at the Proto-Komi stage, so surface u, i, ɯ are heavy or light word by word (etymologically); vowel length, codas and onsets play no role. Itkonen 1955: 28-29 uses the same split in Wiedemann's terms «schwer»/«leicht» (reflexes of Proto-Permic u, i̮, i light, all others heavy).
3990.dflt: Final syllable, per Itkonen 1955: 29: 'Der Akzent ist gewöhnlich in der Silbe zu finden, die den ersten «schweren» Vokal hat. Gibt es nur «leichte» Vokale im Worte, so ist das Wort endbetont' (buzginө· 'schlagen', pөčkiśa·ń 'von innen'). Lytkin 1970: 250 says only that the accent is 'на каком-нибудь гласном непервого слога' (examples muni·s, munө·, both final).
3990.prule: Unbounded, vowel-quality ('качественно-вокальное') stress with no initial default. In polysyllables the first syllable is stressed iff its vowel is 'heavy' = etymologically mid or low (e, o, ȯ, a, and the surface u, ɯ, i that continue Proto-Komi closed mid *o̭, *ȯ̭, *ḙ; p. 252). If the first-syllable vowel is 'light' = etymologically high (i < *i, u < *u, ө < *i̮; ө is phonetically mid today but patterns as high), it is never stressed and the accent lies on a later syllable; Lytkin 1970 says only 'some non-first syllable' (muni·s, munө·), while Itkonen 1955: 29 gives the completing clause: the accent is usually on the syllable with the first heavy vowel, and a word with only light vowels is end-stressed. Monosyllables trivially stressed.

3991.dq: In most Komo nouns, each syllable has a discrete, level tone. (Tone is described per syllable at word level for nouns and verb stems, and at derivational, inflectional and post-lexical strata; stress is never mentioned at any domain.)

3991.prule: Two-level-tone language: every syllable of a word carries a discrete lexical or grammatical tone, H or L (all four HH/HL/LH/LL melodies attested on bisyllabic nouns), plus a rising LH contour on monosyllables; nasals can also bear tone. No word-stress or accent rule is stated anywhere in the source.

3991.tone: The source is a dedicated 90-page tone study (two level tones H/L, rising contour on monosyllables, tone-bearing nasals, three strata of tone rules, downstep, intonation; instrumental appendix on downstep). The words 'stress', 'prominence', 'intensity' and 'loudness' never occur in the tone paper, the 1992 MA thesis or its 2011 SIL re-edition; 'accent' occurs only as 'acute accent' (H-tone diacritic, p. 76) and 'circumflex accent' (footnote 10, foot of p. 81 between the 'page 81' and 'page 82' headers: a diacritic for a branching vowel). 'penultimate' hits concern an unpredictable H in a noun (footnote 8, pp. 80-81) and a falling contour on the penultimate syllable of declarative-final possessives (p. 143, after examples (114)-(117): 'Thus, regardless of dialect, a falling contour is obtained on the penultimate syllable when in the declarative-final position'), not stress. The 2011 re-edition defers tone to the 1992 paper ('A paper on tone has been presented in Thomas 1992'). Webonary 2014 phonology page: 'High, low and rising tones that can carry lexical or grammatical content, Nasals can carry high or low tone, CV and NCV syllables' - no stress.

(the statement governs the citation forms of a wordlist, i.e. words; 'uitgang' = word ending; phrase prominence is not mentioned. 3992.heavy: Not framed as 'heavy' by the source. A final syllable takes the main stress unless it is a 'toonlooze uitgang', i.e. its vowel is the toonlooze ('toonloos zooals in de', 'nauw hoorbare') e written ĕ; so a full-vowel final syllable is stressable and an ĕ-final syllable is not. In the Konerawsch column the breve occurs only on e (tsjirĕ, bandĕr, atsjoerĕ, dewasoedĕ).
3992.dflt: Final syllable whenever its vowel is full (01 001 0001 00001 000001 0000001 00000001). When the final vowel is ĕ, stress is on the penult regardless of the penult's vowel (explicit only in the Marind section p. 9, 'In dat geval valt ook de klemtoon op de voorlaatste'; the N.B. itself says only that the final is skipped). No case of two consecutive reduced final syllables is given.
3992.prule: Main stress on the final syllable unless that syllable is a 'toonlooze uitgang', i.e. ends in the toonlooze (schwa-like, 'nauw hoorbare') e written ĕ; such a final syllable is skipped and stress falls on the penult. The condition is the quality of the final vowel (full vs reduced), which the house scheme codes as weight-sensitive (full-vs-reduced-vowel), not as a quantity-insensitive fixed-final rule with a marked exception class: the N.B. adopts the Marind spelling, in which ĕ is 'de toonlooze e' (as in Dutch 'de', p. 11), and the Marind section gives the same clause with the landing site explicit ('In dat geval valt ook de klemtoon op de voorlaatste', p. 9). The N.B. is a blanket transcriber's convention for all seven bordering-language wordlists (only Digoeleesch excepted, often penultimate); the breve is applied to Konerawsch forms (tsjirĕ 'tand', bandĕr 'slaap', déw atsjoerĕ 'ebbe', dewasoedĕ 'strooming'), always on e.
3992.srule: Secondary stress ('bijklemtoon') alternates trochaically leftward from the final, main-stressed syllable, i.e. on every second syllable counting back from the main stress ('Van de laatste lettergreep verspringt de bijklemtoon trocheevormig naar voren'); 'trocheevormig' is glossed in the same book's Marind stress section (p. 9) as 'afwisselend een betoonde en een onbetoonde lettergreep, b.v.: DIraRI'. Blanket transcriber's note covering the Konerawsch wordlist, not a Koneraw-specific analysis.

3993.prule: No stress rule stated. 3995.tone: Theil (first-hand, 2005-2007 fieldwork): 'Koorete is not a stress or accent language. It has two distinctive word level tones, a rising tone and a falling tone' (minimal pairs ʔáaʃ'e 'curse' / ʔàaʃ'e 'scratch', k'áme 'speak angrily' / k'àme 'become evening', s'óome 'throw' / s'òome 'fast'); rising = pitch rising throughout the word with the last syllable low before pause, falling = slightly falling pitch throughout the word. Theil reports the earlier analyses he rejects: Hayward 1982 'an accentual language, with an accent realized as a heightened pitch'; Ford 1990 'loudness, rather than heightened pitch … is the principle exponent of stress', plus a rare contrastive 'downward gliding tone... which occurs only on stressed syllables'. Azeb Amha 2007 (EAE 3:429-430, the scan excerpt): 'a clear distinction between two tones: high and low, but the occurrence of the high tone in a word is restricted. Because of this, K. is regarded as a tone-accent language.' No accessible source states a position for the accent/H/stress.

3999.prule: Accent position is lexically distinctive and no positional rule is given: minimal pairs kará 'love' vs kára 'moon', dúpui 'he has washed it' vs dupúi 'it has sprouted', puántaansi vs púantaansi, dúmari 'I bathed' vs dumári 'I went home'. The accent is generally weak; some disyllables have both syllables on one pitch level and get no accent mark (dua, karaṅ, mutu, apo, nankai, nantoṅ); in words of three or more syllables accented on the 2nd (or 3rd) syllable, that syllable and all preceding syllables are high-pitched, following syllables low. Stated for Nasioi; Koromira is described 'only insofar as it deviates from the Nasioi dialect' and no deviation in accent is listed, so the statement reaches Koromira by the source's own framing. Rausch's Koromira forms carry accents on different syllables (báro, káiro, nárun, uó, narúnta, kéintakára, bávoroi, bákuri, bávintu, báripi), consistent with a lexical accent but no rule is stated for them.

4002.dq: Trans-Zab exhibits a shift of word stress from the penultimate to the ultimate syllable in the nominal system (with some exceptions, chiefly adverbs)
4002.dloc: Mutzafi 2008: p. 415, sec. 4 'Penultimate > ultimate stress'; transcription note p. 411 fn. 8; JKS = J. Koy Sanjaq, p. 409 fn. 1.
4002.prule: Word stress is conditioned by word class and morphological make-up: in the nominal system (nouns, adjectives) it falls on the final syllable (a Trans-Zab shift from the pan-NENA penultimate; exceptions chiefly adverbs), e.g. nāšá 'man', nawtá 'nit', ganāwá 'thief'. No verbal rule is stated for this dialect; the paper's transcription default is penultimate (fn. 8), and the JKS verb forms it prints are final-stressed when the word ends in the bare present base or in the 1pl. ending -éx (šaqə́l vs J.Zakho šāqəl; ʾabé, ʾalé, ʾamə́r, ʾaxə́l, ʾezə́l, hawə́l, hawé, kawé, yaʾə́l; našqéx) and penultimate when a further suffix follows (šaqəlwa, nšiqle, nešqāle, nešqile, našqexən) and in ʾame, i.e. verbal stress follows the morphological build of the form, not a syllable count. Kim 2008 (citing the grammar, Mutzafi 2004b: 55f.) summarizes the group as final syllable of nominal and verbal STEMS with variable retraction in certain categories (vocatives).

4008.prule: Accent position is fixed by word class and morpheme identity, not by syllable count or weight: nouns carry the accent on the final syllable of the base (p. 26 'Les noms sont accentués sur la syllabe finale'; p. 185 'sur la dernière syllabe des bases de têtes nominales'), with most inflectional suffixes atonic and a listed set of suffixes tonic (plural absolutive -mí/-bí/-mbí and -ar; the genitive in -i of the nouns that take it; the locative -éˤ), so that the accent moves onto a tonic suffix and otherwise stays on the base; all dependent/nominalised verb forms (masdars, gerunds and converbs, substantivised participles; also the future = imperfective participle + copula, and the interrogative forms) are accented on the FINAL syllable; independent finite indicative verb forms (all except the future) and place adverbs on the INITIAL syllable. Attributive adjectives, attributive participles and genitives are proclitic (unaccented); a participle heading an absolutive phrase is tonic but 'perd son accent s'il est épithète' (§19.1.3 p. 345). Accent position distinguishes segmentally identical forms (yi-qr-íc 'to seize' masdar vs yí-qr-ic 'was seized' aorist; xhiyíc 'to become' vs xhíyic 'became'; b-ar-í vs b-ár-i).
4008.srule: None described for simple words: Authier 2009 gives one (pitch) accent per word and says each constituent carries one 'accent de hauteur' (§2.8.2 p. 26; §13.1 p. 185); no secondary or rhythmic accent is mentioned anywhere in the accent passages (pp. 26, 88, 141-144, 155, 185, 345 read). Two accents are reported only for the periphrastic negative future, which keeps the participle's accent and that of the independent negative copula (§10.6 p. 155; ex. 598 p. 159).
4008.quote: Les syllabes non accentuées sont prononcées nettement, sans altération des voyelles. L’accent est mélodique, montant ou descendant, et mériterait plus de recherches. Il n’y a en tout cas pas de tons absolus. Les adjectifs et participes épithètes ainsi que les génitifs sont proclitiques. Les noms sont accentués sur la syllabe finale; quelques suffixes nominaux sont accentués, ainsi les marques de pluriel -mi/-bi et -ar. Comme les formes verbales indépendantes, les adverbes de lieu ont un accent initial, avec un allongement expressif de la première syllabe. La place de l’accent permet de repére…

4008.idn: Source describes the Alik-village dialect (Quba district, NE Azerbaijan) of the Kryz dialect continuum (Kryz, Djek, Alik-Khaput); independent verb forms 'diffèrent considérablement entre les trois dialectes' (p. 141), so the verb-accent statements are Alik usage.
4008.exq_: quelques suffixes nominaux sont accentués, ainsi les marques de pluriel -mi/-bi et -ar. (p. 26) ... Toutes sauf le futur ont un accent initial. (p. 141) ... Le futur est formé du participe imperfectif, qui reste accentué sur la finale, et de la copule (p. 143) ... [formes interrogatives] accentuées…
4008.tone: Authier describes the accent as 'mélodique, montant ou descendant' (p. 26) and as an 'accent de hauteur' (p. 185), says it 'mériterait plus de recherches', and explicitly denies lexical tone ('Il n’y a en tout cas pas de tons absolus'); unaccented syllables show no vowel reduction. Realisation is thus pitch, but placement is a categorical rule by word class, so the record is coded set by morphology rather than tone or pitch accent; a reviewer who codes by realisation could label it pitch-accent.

4016.prule: Williams 2016 (dedicated phonology sketch in a dissertation based on nearly two years of fieldwork (early 2012 to early 2014) in Lantoka, the same village Donohue's data come; Glottolog's grammar sketch for kula1280): word-level stress is not positionally fixed. The author's own examples put stress on the 1st or 2nd syllable of disyllables, on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd of trisyllables and on the penult of quadrisyllables; stress 'apparently makes some limited phonemic contrasts' (hedged: 'further analysis is required'), with the tentative minimal pair /'kula/ 'split in two' vs /ku'la/ 'foam', and is 'potentially phonemic' with low functional load. Reading of this source alone: lexical (hedged), ''.
4016.srule: Secondary stress exists but no placement rule is stated: Williams 2016 marks <ˌ> 'for secondary stress' in his transcriptions, where it falls two syllables from the primary (e.g. [ˌba.lu.'ne] 'sweet potato', [ˌa.da.'ma.sa] 'bird', [ˌgɐ.ka.'ba.ku] 'cat', ['ta.tu.ˌku] 'talk about'); marking of initial-stressed trisyllables is inconsistent (ˈka.pi.ta unmarked). Donohue 1996 does not mention secondary stress.

4016.cfw: Williams 2016, in a dissertation grammar sketch with a table of examples and an apparent minimal pair (/'kula/ 'split in two' vs /ku'la/ 'foam'), shows Kula stress falling on different syllables in different words and possibly contrastive, which outweighs Donohue 1996's single footnote in a syntax article calling stress non-contrastive and initial, though Williams himself says the contrast still needs confirmation.
